gavel for order, and had the prisoner brought in. Ganimard took his seat again in the
courtroom. "Monsieur Baudru, how and when did you come to be at Santé Prison?" the judge gently
asked the prisoner. He did not wish to frighten the man. Baudru seemed to relax. "Two
months ago I was homeless and sleeping on the street," he replied in a weary voice.
"The police put me in a cell at the courthouse overnight. A judge gave me a
warning, and I was released the next day." "Then what happened?" asked Bouvier. "Well, I was
standing outside the courthouse when suddenly I was grabbed by two guards." "And?" the judge prompted.
Baudru shrugged. "They put me into a prison van and took me to Santé Prison. Since then
I’ve been in cell 24." "Lupin’s cell," muttered Bouvier. Baudru shrugged again and said, "Truth be
told, Judge, I was happy in cell 24. I got food, a warm bed, and hot
showers." At Baudru’s response the courtroom burst into laughter. The prisoner was returned to cell 24
until his case could be investigated more thoroughly, and later that evening, Judge Bouvier, Dudouis, and
Ganimard met privately. "We have discovered that the precise day and time Baudru was outside the
courthouse corresponds to the moment Lupin left court for Santé Prison in a prison van," began Dudouis.
"Could the guards have made a mistake?" said the detective. "Perhaps they mistook Baudru for Lupin?"
"Or is Baudru an accomplice?" asked the judge. "You have no grounds to hold Baudru," said
Ganimard. "You must release him. But my men and I will keep him under close surveillance.
If he is working with Lupin, sooner or later he will lead us to him." The
men agreed on this arrangement, and Monsieur Dudouis appointed Inspectors Folenfant and Dieuzy to assist Ganimard
in watching Baudru. A few days later, Désiré Baudru was released from Santé Prison, and the first
thing he did was enter a secondhand-clothing store. He exchanged his tattered jacket and vest for
an old but wearable coat and walked to the bus depot. The bus he wanted to
take was full, so Baudru sat in the waiting room. Just outside the depot, Ganimard gave
instructions to his two assistants. "Men, go and stop a carriage for us. When Baudru gets
on the next bus, we’ll follow him." The two men obeyed. Then Ganimard entered the waiting
room, but it was empty. "I’m an idiot!" cried Ganimard. "I forgot there was another exit." Ganimard
rushed through the rear exit just in time to catch sight of Baudru getting onto another
bus. With no time to give instructions to his assistants, Ganimard had to follow Baudru on
his own. He ran and pulled himself up onto the bus as it left the depot.
"There he is," observed Ganimard. Baudru was already fast asleep on a seat. His mouth was
half open, his head was rolling from side to side, and there was an incredible expression
of stupidity on his smudged face. "This man must be who he says he is," said
Ganimard to himself. "He’s certainly incapable of deceiving anyone." Suddenly Baudru stood up. He got off at
the next stop and started walking leisurely toward a nearby park. He was whistling as if
he were in a good mood. "Ah, he’s glad he’s a free man," Ganimard thought as
he followed close behind. After an hour Baudru finally sat down on a park bench, and
Ganimard continued to watch him from behind a tree. But after thirty minutes, the detective could
stand it no longer. He approached Baudru and sat down next to him. "It’s a beautiful day,"
Ganimard said cheerfully. No response. Then the man threw his head back and laughed merrily. The
hairs on Ganimard’s neck stood up. "I know that laugh!" he thought. Ganimard swiftly grabbed the
man by his collar and looked hard into his face. The twinkling eyes staring back at
him were undeniably Lupin’s. "Arsène Lupin!" he stammered, tightening his hold. Suddenly Lupin made a slight
movement and a surge of pain went up Ganimard’s arm. The detective quickly released his hold.
"If you had taken my martial arts class you would know that with a little more pressure,
I could have broken your arm," Lupin said calmly, straightening his collar. "And you would have
deserved it. I am surprised that you, an old friend, should treat me in such an
abusive way." Ganimard stood there stunned for a moment and then said, "I can’t believe it
was my testimony that allowed Baudru, I mean you, to be released." "My dear Ganimard, do
not take it personally. If it hadn’t been you, I would have arranged for someone else
to testify," Lupin said lightly. "But how did you change your appearance?" whispered Ganimard. "As the judge
kindly mentioned, working alongside Dr. Altier, the bacteriologist, I learned which substances can change skin color
and texture. Hugo, the magician, taught me how to hold my muscles and body a certain
way. Add to that two months of dieting in cell 24, and voilà!" Lupin stood and
spread his arms. "The trick is complete!" "And Baudru?" asked Ganimard. "Oh, he is real—a poor,
harmless fellow. Baudru and I share many similar features, so my friends arranged for him to
be outside the courthouse about the same time I was there." "But there was no substitution," said
Ganimard. "It was me all along, my good man," said Lupin. "An actual substitution would have
been too difficult. So I created the public belief that Arsène Lupin would escape and would
not be present at the trial." "And we believed it too," said Ganimard. "The judge, the
police . . ." "During the trial I admit I had a small worry that I
would be recognized. But you, my reliable friend, spoke with such conviction—‘This man is not Arsène
Lupin!’ Everyone was prepared to believe you." Lupin clapped his hands. Ganimard hung his head. "What do
you plan to do now?" "Well, I will shower, rest, and change into something more presentable.
Tonight I have a most important engagement," Lupin said, turning to leave. "What is it?" asked
Ganimard. "Tonight I dine with the British ambassador!" Lupin walked away and disappeared among the trees.
My friends had invited me to stay at their château on the banks of the
Seine. First, I would travel by rail to the Rouen station, where my automobile would
be waiting for me. Then I would drive the remaining distance. I boarded the
train in Paris, but the passengers in my compartment were smoking, an awful habit. So
I took my overcoat, newspaper, and timetable and sought refuge in a neighboring compartment. It
was occupied by a woman who scrutinized me suspiciously as I entered. I smiled and
had just settled into my seat when the door suddenly opened and a man rushed
in. The woman let out a small cry and clenched her handkerchief. The man
was dressed elegantly; I noticed his stylish silk shirt and leather gloves. He was young
and handsome, and there was something vaguely familiar about his face. The whistle sounded as
the train pulled out of the station, and I turned to look at the woman.
"Are you ill, madame?" I asked, because her face was devoid of all color. Her
frightened eyes met mine. "Monsieur . . . ," she whispered in a trembling voice,
"that man . . ." She nodded slightly toward the newcomer, who had settled
on a seat and appeared to be sleeping. "Do you recognize him?" "No. Why do
you ask?" I whispered back. She leaned toward me. "He is Arsène Lupin." I looked
at the sleeping gentleman again; he seemed perfectly harmless. "Madame, that isn’t plausible," I assured
her. "Just yesterday, a large reward was announced for Lupin’s capture. Surely, he would not
be so imprudent as to make a public appearance the day after." The woman’s
voice grew a bit louder. "My husband is a director with the prison system. He
received word that police were searching for Arsène Lupin at the Paris train station." "Yet
he allowed you to board this train?" "Lupin was said to be traveling to Nice,"
she replied less confidently. "But he must have switched trains." "Madame, don’t be afraid," I
said. "Even if Lupin is aboard this train, the last thing he wants to
do is draw attention to himself." My words did not reassure her, and she turned
her face to the window. I opened my newspaper and read reports of Lupin’s trial,
but I soon lost interest. I drifted into a deep slumber and dreamed of Arsène
Lupin as a menacing black shape coming toward me, growing larger and larger. With a
cry, I awoke to find our traveling companion had leaped on top of me and
now had his knee on my chest. One hand was around my throat, and
the other was rummaging through my pockets for my wallet. "Keep still and I won’t
hurt you," he said as I started to choke. He took a rope out of
his pocket and quickly tied me up. The man turned to the woman. "Madame, give
me your handkerchief," he commanded in a calm but threatening voice. He stuffed the handkerchief
into my mouth, and within moments, I was bound, gagged, and helpless. The man
was cool, deft, and audacious: traits possessed by the gentleman burglar himself—Arsène Lupin! But he
was not Arsène Lupin, because Lupin was the man lying on the floor, gagged and
bound. Yes, I was the helpless victim! "Give me your purse," the thief said to
the frightened woman. "My jewels are in there," she sobbed as she reluctantly handed him
her purse. "Take off your rings too," he ordered. Trembling with fear, she pulled
the rings from her fingers and handed them to the thief. Then she fainted. He
put her rings and my wallet into the purse. I thought: "Here I am, Arsène
Lupin, robbed like an unsophisticated novice." As I lay there, I pondered the various problems
this situation presented. First, that man now had my wallet. The money was not important,
but the wallet held papers containing information—the names of my associates, plans, addresses, and other
documents—that could lead to my capture. I was going to visit friends who knew
me by the name Guillaume Berlat, and my likeness to Lupin was always a source
of jokes to them, so I wore no disguise. I knew the Rouen police would
question me, but I had a fake identity card in my wallet saying I was
a deputy police officer. However, now I was no longer free, had no identity card,
and could not use any of my usual tricks. Plus, the woman would scream
the minute someone opened the compartment door once the train stopped. "What am I going
to do?" I thought. "Ah, just what I need," the man said as he scanned
my timetable. He found what he was looking for, strode to the window, and looked
out. "Surely, he is not going to jump," I thought. The train was moving at
an alarming speed, but then it slowed down as it entered a tunnel. "Oh,
it’s raining," muttered the man, and he took the woman’s umbrella and put on my
overcoat. Then he left our compartment, and just as the train slowed almost to a
halt, he jumped out the door of the train. "He stole my jewels!" screamed the
woman as the train started to speed up again. The distraught woman was weeping over
her lost possessions without a care for me lying there. I gave her an imploring
look and she quickly removed my gag. "I’ll untie you too," she said. "No,
the police must see everything as it is," I replied. "Monsieur," she cried, "didn’t I
say he was on this train?" "Don’t worry, the police will catch him." "Catch Lupin?
How?" she sniffed. "Listen carefully, madame, and do as I tell you," I began. "When
we arrive in Rouen, the police will come and you must tell them everything that
happened. Give a description . . . his silk shirt, facial features, your umbrella,
his gray overcoat—" "Your coat," she interjected. "No, you are mistaken," I replied hastily. "I
don’t think he had a coat," she said. "It must be his, because it was
not mine. Give your name and your husband’s position. That will make them search more
zealously." "And you?" "I am Guillaume Berlat. If necessary, tell them you know me, that
I’m a friend of your husband. That will save time and will accelerate the
investigation. The important thing is capturing Arsène Lupin and recovering your jewels!" I insisted. When
the train arrived at Rouen station, an officer opened our compartment and the woman gave
an account of what had occurred. "Poor Monsieur Berlat, my husband’s dear friend, was brutally
assaulted," she cried. I was immensely proud of her performance. "But what happened to Lupin?"
asked the officer as he untied me. "He jumped off the train," she continued. "He
was wearing a silk shirt—" "Like Monsieur Berlat’s?" asked the officer, glancing at me.
"Yes, and he had a gray overcoat . . ." She paused and glanced at
me. I held my breath. "We received a telegram saying Lupin wore a gray overcoat,"
said the police officer, nodding. I was taken to the station physician, and after a
brief examination, I was pronounced "shaken, but in strong spirits." Then I approached the Rouen
police chief and his officers on the platform. In a weak voice, I said,
"Sirs, this was indeed the work of Lupin. And if we hurry, I think I
can help." And that is how Arsène Lupin came to be searching for Arsène Lupin!
My plan to capture the thief, recover my papers, and then make my escape had to
be thorough. I told the officers about "Lupin" consulting my timetable. "Lupin leaped off the train
in the tunnel, which is close by the Darnétal station," I explained. "He will probably take
the train that goes to Amiens, since that is the next train. It leaves the station at
10:20"—I glanced at my watch—"exactly 22 minutes from now." "Really, monsieur," said one officer, as they
stared at me in amazement. "That is a marvelous deduction." Perhaps I had been too clever.
I didn’t want them to be suspicious, so I laughed and said, "Ah, nothing sharpens the
mind like having one’s wallet stolen." Then I dared to proceed with my bold suggestions. "My
automobile is here at the station, and if you permit me the assistance of two of
your men, we can intercept Lupin at Darnétal," I said, addressing the police chief. The police
chief hesitated, but at that precise moment, my companion came to my rescue. "I beg you,
listen to Monsieur Berlat," she implored, a fresh wave of tears rolling down her cheeks. Her intervention
was decisive, no doubt because her husband was a man of importance. So the police chief
assigned two officers, named Massol and Delivet, to accompany me. We raced off in my automobile,
but unfortunately, we arrived at Darnétal Station three minutes too late. However, after talking to the
stationmaster, Massol found out that a man in a gray overcoat had indeed purchased a ticket
for Amiens and boarded the departed train. "The train is an express," said Delivet, "but the
next stop is in a mere 19 minutes. If we do not reach that stop before
Lupin, we can proceed to Amiens." "How far is it to the next station?" I asked. "It’s
23 kilometers," he replied. "Hmm, 19 minutes . . ." I made mental calculations. "We will
arrive ahead of him!" We hopped in the automobile, and I pushed hard on the gas
pedal. We flew; the wheels barely touched the ground. "Turn right here!" shouted Delivet. As we
made the turn, we saw a column of black smoke. It was the train! I pressed
harder on the gas and raced side by side against the black monster. We reached the
station just as the train came to a halt at the platform. A few passengers exited
the train, but the thief was not among them. "He must have seen us!" I cried
in frustration. "He probably leaped from the train as it pulled into the station!" "Look! There he
is!" Delivet pointed to a figure crossing the tracks. I started in pursuit, followed by the
two officers. But Massol proved to be an exceptional runner and quickly disappeared into a grove
of trees the thief had just entered. Delivet and I finally reached Massol a few minutes
later, and he motioned for us to be quiet. "There’s an abandoned barn back there," Massol
whispered, barely out of breath. "That’s where Lupin is. He hasn’t seen me." Gasping, I motioned
to Delivet. "Go get help. He may be armed and dangerous." Removing both officers from the
area was imperative to my escape plan. Delivet did as he was told and retreated to
the station. "Monsieur Berlat, you remain here," Massol whispered. "This is a matter for the police." "I
appreciate that," I replied. "However, I am the only one who can recognize the man. I
am willing to risk my life to ensure Lupin is caught for good!" Massol saluted my
bravery and handed me a pistol. "Shoot once if you are in distress, and we will
come to your rescue, sir." Massol hid himself behind a tall tree while I cautiously approached
the barn. The door was slightly open and I could hear sounds of movement from within.
I entered quietly and quickly familiarized myself with the surroundings. His back was turned toward me.
In two strides, I was upon him. He tried to fire a revolver that he held in
his hand. But he had no time. I threw him to the ground in such a
manner that his arms were pinned beneath him. Twisted and helpless, I held him down with
my knee on his chest. "Listen, my boy," I began. "I am Arsène Lupin. I will
let you up if you hand me, slowly and carefully, my wallet with all items intact,
and the woman’s jewels. In return, I will save you from the police and enlist you
as one of my associates. Answer, yes or no." "Yes," he replied quickly. "Very good," I
said as I freed him and we both stood up. "Your escape this morning displayed exceptional
precision and courage. I admire that." Suddenly, he pulled a large knife from his trousers and lunged
at me. "Fool!" I exclaimed as I easily sidestepped his attack and gave him a sharp
blow to the neck. He fell, stunned. I recovered my wallet, all my papers, and the
woman’s purse from the overcoat pocket. Curious, I also pulled out the thief’s wallet and found
an envelope with his name on it: Pierre Onfrey. Now, I realized why his face had
seemed familiar on the train. I had seen his picture in the newspaper; he was a
wanted murderer who had cut the throats of a woman and her two daughters. "I must
hurry," I said to myself. I put some money into an envelope with a card bearing these
words: From Arsène Lupin to his worthy assistants, Massol and Delivet, with gratitude. I placed the
envelope where it would be easily noticed and then rummaged through the woman’s purse. She had
a few choice pieces of jewelry, which I instinctively pocketed, and I left her a ring
made of green glass and a diamond pendant which did not appeal to my tastes. "What
is that saying?" I thought, smiling to myself. "‘You can take the lion out of the
jungle, but you cannot take the jungle out of the lion.’ Or was it a tiger?"
I carefully placed the purse next to the letter as Pierre began to stir. I prayed
that Delivet had followed my orders to alert the other officers at the station and that they
were nearby. I took the pistol Massol had given me and shot once into the air.
Then I swiftly left the barn through a back door. As I ran away, I heard
the voices of Delivet and Massol calling out for me. Smiling, I crossed through the forest
and found my automobile just where I had left it, unguarded and ready to transport me
away. Later that evening, I arrived back in Paris and telegraphed my friends that I would
not be visiting after all. The following morning, the Écho printed this sensational item: Dramatic events
transpired yesterday. Arsène Lupin initiated the arrest of the vicious murderer Pierre Onfrey. Being a gentleman,
Lupin also restored to Madame Renaud her purse, which had been stolen by Onfrey, and he also
gave generous compensation to the two detectives who assisted him in making the arrest. Lupin related
this to me over a shared bottle of wine. Regrettably, some particulars have been omitted because
my friend would be most displeased if I were to disclose every detail of his dealings.
The colorful history of the piece of jewelry known as "the Queen’s Necklace" started with its
creation for Madame Du Barry, the last mistress of King Louis XV. Later, this necklace was
owned by a cardinal who intended to give it to Marie Antoinette, the queen of France, before
her head was so brutally removed from her neck. After passing through many hands over the
years, and with only a few of the original diamonds remaining, the necklace was bought and
restored by Gaston de Dreux-Soubise, the nephew of the cardinal. Although the Dreux-Soubise family’s financial fortunes
dwindled with each generation, the family continued to take pride in the ownership of such a
magnificent necklace. Nearly a century later, Count Dreux-Soubise was keeping the necklace in a safety-deposit box at
the bank. He removed it only for special occasions. One night, the count took the necklace
out for his wife to wear to a royal reception for the king of Denmark. Everyone
who attended commented on how the beauty of the countess was enhanced by the sparkling jewels.
Afterward, the count and countess returned home, tired but elated by the attention the necklace and,
consequently, they too, had received. "I hate to take it off," the countess said as she walked
into their bedroom, touching the necklace around her neck. "Ah, there will be other occasions for
you to impress royalty," said the count. The countess removed the necklace and handed it to
her husband, who carefully placed it in a red leather case. The count opened the door
of a large closet that had been specially constructed to house the necklace when it was
in their possession. He placed the box on a high shelf amid hatboxes and stacks of linen,
closed the door, and retired to bed. The next morning, the count arose intending to return
the necklace to the bank before breakfast. However, he was called to the stables about a
sick horse and was detained longer than he had anticipated. Finally, he went to the closet
to retrieve the necklace. "Back so soon from the bank?" His wife was up and getting
her hair done by her maid. "No, I’ll be leaving shortly," he replied as he rummaged
around in the closet. The count reappeared with a curious expression. "Did you move it, dearest?" "Move
what?" asked his wife with a puzzled smile. Then, understanding the situation, her face lost all
color. "The necklace," said the count, stunned. "It’s not here." His wife, pins sticking oddly out
of her hair, jumped up. "You must be mistaken . . ." "No, I’m not mistaken,"
he cried, throwing boxes and linens out of the closet. "I put it here on this
shelf." They searched the entire closet, but the necklace was gone. Resigned, the count called the police,
and Inspector Valorbe arrived promptly. "Are you sure no one entered your bedroom last night?" asked
Valorbe after examining the closet. "I am absolutely certain," the count said emphatically. "Besides, our room
was bolted from the inside. I had to unbolt it this morning for my wife’s maid."
"There is no other entrance into your closet?" inquired the inspector. "No," replied the count. "Windows?"
Valorbe took a candle into the closet. "Yes, one, but it is closed up," said the count,
pointing to a small window. The lower half was covered by a narrow curtain. "What is
outside the window?" asked Valorbe. "A small inner courtyard," the count answered. "Is there a floor
above this?" "There are two floors—most of the servants live there," explained the count. "But there
is an iron grate over the court between this floor and the one above. That’s why
this closet is so dark." Valorbe removed the curtain and saw that the window was fastened. No
one could have entered that way. "Did any of your servants know that you wore the
necklace last night?" asked the inspector, turning to the countess. "Certainly," she replied. "But no one
knew it was hidden in the closet, except . . ." "Who, madame?" asked Valorbe. "Henriette,"
the countess said a little louder, looking at her husband. "Who is she?" asked the inspector.
"We went to school together," began the countess. "Her family disowned her for marrying a working-class boy.
After he died, she needed a place for her and her son." The countess’ chin lifted
slightly in pride. "She is good with a needle, so I said she could live here
and work for me." Valorbe and the countess went to Henriette’s apartment, which was on the
same floor. Henriette was sewing, and her six-year-old son, Raoul, was sitting next to her, reading.
"My God!" the inspector thought when he saw how Henriette and her son lived. The small, dark
room was hardly larger than a broom closet, and an even smaller room served as a
kitchen. The place was wretched. "I can’t believe it!" Henriette cried upon hearing of the theft.
"Could a thief have passed through your rooms, madame?" asked Valorbe. "That’s impossible," Henriette replied. "I
never go out." The boy stared at Valorbe with eyes that resembled his mother’s. "And look,"
she added as she opened her kitchen window. "It is at least three meters to the ledge
of that closet window." "Who told you the thief might have entered through that window?" the
inspector asked pointedly. Henriette replied in a puzzled voice, "That’s the closet window, is it not?
The necklace was in there." "How did you know that?" Valorbe persisted. "I have always known
it was kept there the night after a party. The countess told me." The woman’s face,
though still young, bore unmistakable traces of sorrow. She drew her son toward her as if
some danger threatened them, and the child kissed his mother’s hand tenderly. All that week, the investigation
continued. Inspector Valorbe questioned the servants, reexamined the bolt and the closet window, and explored every
inch of the small courtyard. The bolt had not been tampered with, and the window could
not have been opened or closed from the outside. It was determined that Henriette had left
the house only four times in the last three years and that the countess treated her
very harshly. The case was closed due to lack of evidence and because the presiding judge secretly
believed the count and countess had sold the necklace due to their poor financial situation. Even
though Henriette had not been charged in the theft, the countess fired her. As their income
continued to drop, the count and countess had to sell off many of their possessions. Creditors
kept calling to ask them for money, which they did not have. They would have been
totally ruined if they had not inherited money from relatives. Some months after Henriette was fired, the
countess received a strange letter from her former schoolmate: Madame, I do not know how to
thank you! It was you, wasn’t it? Puzzled, the countess wrote back, asking Henriette what her
letter meant. I have received two banknotes worth one thousand francs each. If you didn’t send
them, who did? No one else knows where I live. The next year, Henriette received another
letter containing two thousand francs, and a third and fourth. However, the value of the notes doubled
in value for the fifth and sixth years. These last two letters were signed "Anquety" and
"Péchard." The return addresses were false. After six years, Henriette died, and the mystery remained unsolved.
More than two decades had passed since the mysterious disappearance of the Queen’s Necklace. Count
de Dreux-Soubise and his wife had traveled widely, maintaining a moderate social standing by
inheriting from distant relatives. But one day, the couple decided to return to Paris and
hold a dinner party at their old estate. Among the invited guests were the count’s
nieces, a cousin, the mayor of Le Vésinet, an Italian military officer named Floriani
whom the count had met in Sicily, and General Marquis de Rouzières, an old friend.
After the meal, coffee was served, and as was usual in the presence of
the count and countess, the conversation turned toward the missing necklace. Each guest had a
theory of how the theft had been carried out. "Monsieur Floriani," said the countess, "what
is your opinion?" "Oh madame, I have none," Floriani replied graciously. "Nonsense! Surely, you
have a theory," insisted the general. Floriani cleared his throat awkwardly. "I must admit, I
have sometimes unraveled mysteries that have baffled even the greatest of detectives, though I am
no Sherlock Holmes." He chuckled. "But I’m unfamiliar with the affair of the Queen’s
Necklace." Everyone then turned to the count, who told the story. Floriani listened carefully, asked
a few questions, and then said, "It is indeed a strange case, yet quite simple—"
"Simple?" barked the general. "This case left Paris’ cleverest police clueless!" "It is simple
because we are faced with one fact. The thief could only have entered by the
bedroom door or the closet window," said Floriani mildly. "A person cannot open a bolted
door from the outside. Therefore, the thief must have entered through the window." The
count shook his head. "The window was closed and fastened." Floriani ignored the count’s remark
and continued. "To enter through the window, the thief simply had to construct some
kind of bridge between Henriette’s kitchen window and the closet window ledge." "But the window
was fastened," repeated the count. "Possibly, but did the window have a small, hinged opening
at the top, a transom?" asked Floriani. "How did you know that?" the count
said. "Many older houses have transom windows, and without a transom, the theft cannot be
explained." "But the transom was closed, like the window." The count frowned. "No, it wasn’t,"
said Floriani. "If you had looked closely, you would have seen that it had
been opened." "How?" asked the count. "Most transoms open by means of a wire with
a ring at the end, no?" Floriani said. The count nodded. "Through a hole in
the window, a person could pull the wire down using, for example, a poker
hooked at the end, and open the transom," continued Floriani. The count laughed. "Excellent! Your
theory is very creative. But there was no hole in the window." Floriani said
quite seriously, "Yes, there was." "Nonsense, we would have seen it," argued the count. "Only
if you were looking for it," Floriani replied. "I am certain there is a hole
in the putty in the side of the window." The guests began murmuring among
themselves as the count wiped perspiration from his forehead. "How can you, without even seeing
where the theft took place, make such a statement?" the count demanded. "You are contradicting
everything we know about this case." Floriani shrugged. "It is only my theory. If
I am wrong, you can easily prove it." "I will do so at once," said
the count and abruptly left the room. Not a single word was said until the
count returned to his guests. "My love, what did you find?" the countess eagerly
asked her husband. The count merely shook his head in disbelief. "What is it, man?"
The general shook his friend’s arm. The count took a deep breath. "There is a
hole on the side of the window, just as Floriani said." All eyes turned
to Floriani. "Please tell us the rest of your theory," implored the count. Floriani took
a sip of his drink and calmly went on. "I think the thief knew
the countess was going to wear the necklace that evening. He prepared his bridge ahead
of time, perhaps using some boards from a kitchen shelf. He waited until you retired,
and then he crawled across the wooden bridge, pushed the poker through the putty,
and pulled the transom ring." "But the window lock was too far down to reach.
How could he have opened the window?" asked the countess. Floriani paused, and then said,
"He must have crawled in through the transom." "Impossible!" exclaimed the count. "It’s too
small. No man could fit through such an opening." "Then the thief must have been
a child," Floriani declared. The countess gasped, and her hand flew to her heart. "Henriette
had a son . . . Raoul," the count recalled. "Henriette must have forced
her son to do it!" cried the countess. Floriani shook his head. "No, she had
nothing to do with it." "But how could she not know?" retorted the countess.
"It must have happened during the night, while she was sleeping. Moreover, you said Henriette
thanked you for the banknotes she had received." Floriani paused; his voice became chilly. "Would
she have done that if she were an accomplice to this theft?" The guests
shook their heads. "Of course not," Floriani asserted. "But the child could have gone to
a dealer, sold a diamond every year, and arranged for the money to be sent
to his mother." "And after Henriette died," said the countess, "what happened to the
necklace?" "Oh, I expect the boy kept it as a memento." Floriani smiled. "Congratulations on
your vivid imagination!" the count said, attempting to lighten the mood. "I imagine nothing," Floriani
replied. "I only explain events as they must have occurred." "But what can you
know of these events?" whispered the countess. Floriani turned to her coolly. "From what you
have told me, I have a good idea of what kind of life the
mother and son had here. I can understand how the conditions they lived under and
how they were treated could affect a young boy. He saw his mother suffer through
the theft accusations, her illness, and consequently, her death. Years roll on. The boy
became a man who desired very much to meet the people who had treated his
mother so badly." Floriani’s tone and manner had changed dramatically. Tension permeated the room. "Who
are you, monsieur?" the count asked suspiciously. "I am Floriani, a man you met
in Sicily. I only attempted to depict what Henriette’s son might have felt. The boy
did what he did because he could not stand to see his mother suffer any
longer." His voice cracked with emotion. No one doubted now that Floriani was Henriette’s
son, but what could the count and countess do about it? Who would believe that
one of the greatest unsolved mysteries of all time was committed by an angry child?
The count tried to recapture the earlier lighthearted mood of the evening. "Your story
is most entertaining," he said. "But I wonder what has become of Raoul? I hope
he has not abandoned his career as a thief after such a dazzling debut."
Floriani’s eyes twinkled brightly, and he let out a laugh. "Oh, I am certain he
has not." A few days later, the Écho published a sensational article that read: The
historic Queen’s Necklace stolen from the Dreux-Soubise family has been returned to its owner
by Arsène Lupin. Words of praise are not enough to commend such an honorable act.
People often ask me how I met Arsène Lupin, because I know so many intimate details
about him. Some people wonder if I am the mysterious gentleman burglar. Well, I’m very flattered,
but I am not he. However, I will tell you how I came to know
him. In a word, it was chance. On the evening of June 22, I was dining
with some friends at one of Paris’ most charming restaurants. While the other patrons ate, danced,
and laughed, our table was preoccupied with crimes, thefts, and unsolved mysteries. After dinner, my friend
Jean Daspry and I said good-bye to our dinner companions, the Saint-Martins, and walked home.
When we arrived at the little house I’d been renting for a year, Daspry turned to
me and said, "Aren’t afraid? Your house is so isolated. I would be frightened, especially after
what we talked about all night." I didn’t want to admit it, but I was a
bit frightened. We shook hands, and I entered my dark, chilly home. I quickly ascended the
stairs to my bedroom and locked the door. After lighting a candle, I found my
revolver and placed it beside my bed. I changed, got into bed, and picked up my
book from the night table. To my surprise, an envelope addressed to me fell out. I
tore it open and read its contents: From the moment you read this letter, whatever happens,
whatever you may hear, do not make a move or make a sound. If you
do, you are doomed. My heart pounded as I read and reread the letter. Was this
some kind of joke? "This is nonsense!" I thought. "I’ll blow out my candle and go
to sleep." But I could not do it. "Do not make a move," the letter had
said. Suddenly, I heard the floor creak, and then a crackling noise. It was coming
from the library, located two doors from my bedroom. I wanted to grab my gun, but
I saw the window curtain move. I held my breath. It moved again; this time, I
noticed a bulky mass that prevented the curtain from hanging straight. Someone was in my room,
making sure I heeded the words of the letter. One movement, one sound, and I would
be dead. Throughout the night, I heard the most frightening noises coming from the library.
It sounded like the walls were being torn down. Not knowing what was happening fueled the
fear in me as I sat paralyzed in bed, my eyes fixed on the bulky curtain.
Finally, the morning sun seeped through the window, and I heard the familiar bell of the
milk wagon on the boulevard. That gave me courage to make my move. I grabbed
my revolver, aimed at the curtain, and fired. I rushed to the window, but there was
no one there! All night, I had been deceived by a fold in the curtain. Angry,
I unlocked my door and ran to the library. Once again, I was stunned, for everything—furniture,
books, pictures—was in its proper place. There was no trace of any intruders. "This is unbelievable!"
I shouted, rubbing my eyes. Suddenly, something caught my eye. Sticking out from under a
small Persian rug was a card—a playing card. "It’s an ordinary seven of hearts," I said,
picking it up. But I noticed something unusual. At the point of each of the seven
hearts was a hole, as if the card had been pierced by a sharp object. I
put the card in my pocket. I spent the entire day in the library, carefully
examining every inch of the room. It was an ornate room with mosaics on the walls.
One image depicted a Roman god, and another showed a medieval king with a sword. There
was a large window that a man could enter with the aid of a ladder, but
the ladder would have made marks in the soft earth outside. There were no marks.
Without evidence, I could not tell the police what had happened. Who would believe me? However,
being a reporter for Gil Blas had its advantages. I wrote a lengthy account of the
bizarre evening, and the paper published it the next day. Only Daspry seemed to take an
interest in this strange affair; he quickly came to see me. I told him what had
happened. A few days later, I had an unexpected visitor. The gentleman would not give
his name. "I read your article in Gil Blas , and it interested me very much,"
he said. "Thank you," I replied, leading him into the library. "Are the facts you related
exactly as they happened?" the man asked. I nodded. "Then you must leave me alone in
this room," he said. I looked at him in surprise. "Certain details of your account
bear an extraordinary resemblance to another case I’m familiar with. I can reveal further details only
after I have determined for myself whether these two cases are connected. To do that, I
must be alone," said the man nervously but firmly. "How much time do you need?" I
asked. "Only three minutes," he replied. I went downstairs, took out my watch, and began counting.
One minute passed, and then two. I began to feel uneasy, so I started back
up the stairs. Suddenly, I heard a gunshot. I raced to the library and found the
man lying in the middle of the floor, a bullet wound in his forehead. His revolver
lay close by, but another object near the body attracted my attention. It was a playing
card—another seven of hearts. The pointed end of each heart also had a small, round
hole. Soon, the police arrived along with Monsieur Dudouis, chief of the Paris police. "I did
not touch the body," I explained and told them what had happened. The preliminary examination was
brief. The police searched the body, but there were no papers in the pockets of the
deceased, no name on his clothes—nothing to give any clue to the man’s identity. "Did
this man come into my house just to commit suicide?" I thought. "There must have been
something in this room that caused him to kill himself. What had he seen? What frightful
secret had been revealed to him?" "There is nothing missing from the room?" asked Dudouis. "No,
not that I can see," I said. We watched silently as two policemen prepared to put
the body on a stretcher. As they lifted the body, something fell from the left
hand. It was a crumpled card. "‘Georges Andermatt, 37, Rue de Berry, tel: 415.21,’" said Dudouis,
reading the card. "The Paris banker?" I asked. "This is he?" Dudouis leaned over the body
and shook his head. "No, Monsieur Andermatt is older, thinner. Do you have a telephone?" "Of
course. Come with me," I replied. We went into the next room, and Dudouis dialed
the number from the card. "Monsieur Andermatt? This is Dudouis, chief of the Paris police. I
request your presence, sir. Please come at once to 102 Boulevard Maillot. It is very important."
Monsieur Andermatt arrived twenty minutes later, and he was taken to see the body.
"He is Etienne Varin," Andermatt said in a low voice. "You know him?" asked Monsieur
Dudouis. "Just by sight. I know his brother Alfred," said Andermatt. "He came to
see me about a business matter once . . . I forget what it was."
"Do you know any reason why he would commit suicide?" asked Dudouis. "No." "He
held your card in his hand," said Dudouis. "I’m greatly surprised that my card
was found here," Andermatt replied. "I have told you all I know. I sincerely hope
this puzzle is cleared up during the investigation." But the puzzle was not cleared
up. The investigation established that the Varin brothers had led their lives under various
names, frequented gambling resorts, and were possibly involved with a series of robberies. They hadn’t
been seen for the last six years. The case seemed too complicated to me,
so I decided not to waste any time on it. But my friend Daspry became
more and more interested. "Look at this," said Daspry, handing me a foreign newspaper
a few days later. The paper provided an interesting piece of information, possibly connected
to the suicide of Etienne Varin. "‘The first trial of the new submarine will be
launched in a secret location in the presence of the German emperor,’" I read
aloud. "That submarine was supposed to revolutionize naval warfare," Daspry said. "But, my friend,
look at the name of the submarine!" "The Seven-of-Hearts !" I exclaimed. "It also says
here the submarine was designed by French engineers." I wondered if there was a
connection to the events in my home. Then Daspry showed me a copy of the
Écho and said, "This article, titled ‘The Affair of the Seven-of-Hearts,’ was written by
someone named Salvator, and it will shed light on this mysterious case." Clearing his
throat, he then read the entire article aloud. The story revealed that ten years ago,
a young engineer named Louis Lacombe had rented number 102 Boulevard Maillot. "That’s my
house!" I interjected. Daspry nodded and kept reading: Lacombe was working on plans for
a revolutionary submarine. The Varin brothers introduced Lacombe to Georges Andermatt, a banker with many
government connections. Lacombe explained his submarine invention and Andermatt agreed to speak to the
minister of the navy about buying Lacombe’s plans. For two years, Lacombe worked on his
submarine, and he frequently visited the Andermatt home, growing closer to the family. Finally,
Lacombe was ready to submit his work, and one evening, dined at the Andermatt
home. He left there at eleven thirty and disappeared. "What about the submarine plans?" I
cried anxiously. Daspry raised his finger to silence me and read on: After much
investigation, I, Salvator, have discovered that the plans for the Seven-of-Hearts ended up in
the hands of the Varin brothers. "But one of them is dead," I interrupted. "The
article goes on to say that the plans were sold to Germany, and the
Seven-of-Hearts has already been constructed." "Those scoundrels!" I exclaimed. "Wait, my friend," said Daspry. "Salvator
writes that the launch of the Seven-of-Hearts was not successful, and he adds, ‘It
is believed the Varin brothers were missing a final document, and this was the
document Lacombe had in his possession the night he disappeared. Without this document, the plans
are incomplete and therefore worthless.’ The news story ends with a call for Andermatt
to come forward and address these allegations." "Who is Salvator?" I asked. "How does
he know so much?" Daspry shrugged and said, "Whoever he is, he is brave to
bring these facts to the public’s attention." After Salvator’s article appeared, an army of
reporters descended upon the banker’s home, asking questions about his involvement in the suicide. A
few days later, Daspry and I were dining at my house when the door
suddenly opened and a lady entered. She was wearing a veil. "I apologize for
this intrusion," she said before I had a chance to speak. She went to the
window and pulled the curtain closed. Her manner indicated she was familiar with the
surroundings. But how could that be? "I am here on an urgent matter," said
the lady, raising her veil. "I am Madame Andermatt." "Andermatt!" I cried, astonished. "I have
come hoping to obtain information." "There’s nothing I can tell you," I said, "that
hasn’t already been printed in the newspaper. I wish I could help . . ."
There was a moment of silence; she seemed embarrassed and nervous. Daspry suddenly stepped
forward. "May I ask a few personal questions?" "Yes, you may," she said quietly.
"Did you know Louis Lacombe?" Madame Andermatt’s face reddened. "He had business with my husband."
"When was the last time you saw him?" asked Daspry. "The night he disappeared."
She pressed a handkerchief to her eyes. "Do you believe the Varin brothers had
something to do with his disappearance?" Daspry continued. "I am certain they did," she said.
"When Louis, I mean, Monsieur Lacombe, left our house, he had his briefcase, which
contained his papers. A few days later, my husband met with the Varins and discovered
they had Louis’ papers. So they must have taken them from him." "Why didn’t
your husband tell the police?" I interrupted. Madame Andermatt lowered her eyes. "There was
something else in the briefcase." "What?" I cried impatiently. Daspry gave me a stern look
and turned back to the woman. "The Varin brothers used the other item to
blackmail your husband. Your husband, desiring to recover that item, was forced to keep
silent about Lacombe and his papers." The woman nodded sadly. "That item," continued Daspry, "was
a stack of love letters between you and Lacombe, was it not?" I gasped
loudly. "Yes, and Alfred Varin threatened to publish them if my husband told anyone they
had the plans," Madame Andermatt cried. "Varin said the letters were in a secret
safe. But I believe my husband was able to discover that hiding place." "Where
is it?" I asked. "Here." "Here?" I repeated. "Louis Lacombe was a genius and amused
himself by designing safes and locks during his leisure time. My husband believed the
Varin brothers used one of Lacombe’s safes to conceal the papers and letters." "You
mean the plans and letters are here?" I said, in wonderment. "Not now," she said.
"I believe my husband recovered them on the night of June 22. He came
to this house, opened the safe, and left his card to inform the brothers he
feared them no more. Two days later, after reading the article in Gil Blas
, Etienne Varin came, found the safe empty, and killed himself." Daspry thought a
moment and then said, "A good theory, madame, but it was not your husband who
entered this house on June 22." "Who, then?" she exclaimed. "There is a mysterious
individual who is managing this affair. He holds the answers in his hand. It
was he and his friends who entered this house that night and discovered the safe."
"Daspry, who is it?" I asked insistently. "The one who has revealed convincing details
no one else could know and the one who has discovered the secrets of the
Varin brothers. The same one who published his findings in the Écho : Salvator!"
Madame Andermatt became upset when Daspry mentioned Salvator. "He has my letters!" she cried.
"What am I to do?" "Write to him," urged Daspry. "Say that your husband has
the document that completes the submarine plans—because I believe your husband does possess that
document. Confide in Salvator. Tell him you need your letters." Madame thanked us and promised
to keep us informed. Two days later, she sent us a note she had
received: Have not found the letters, but I will get them. Rest easy. I am
watching everything. – Salvator The handwriting was the same as that in the note
I had found in my book on June 22. "You’re right," I told Daspry. "Salvator
is managing this affair." Daspry smiled modestly. "Soon, we will unravel this mystery." "But
what about the two playing cards?" I asked. "I’m not concerned about those now," said
Daspry. "I must find Madame Andermatt’s letters!" For days, Daspry furiously searched the house,
inside and out, but he found nothing. Then, one day, he came to me with
a pickax and shovel. "Come," he ordered, and we began digging behind the house.
We labored for an hour without success. I was discouraged and wanted to give up
when Daspry suddenly cried out. "At last!" His pickax had hit some bones, the
remains of a skeleton with scraps of clothing still hanging from it. I felt sick
to my stomach. Next to the bones was a small, rectangular iron plate. He
picked it up and scraped the dirt off. "It’s the exact size of a playing
card," I remarked. The plate had red spots, and each spot was pierced with
a round hole in the same position as the holes on the sevens of hearts
we had found. I felt unwell after the discovery of the skeleton, so I
rested for a few days while Daspry continued his search for the letters in the
library. For hours, he would tap, tap, tap on the walls, hoping to find
the secret hiding place. On the morning of the third day, I received a curious
letter. The drama that began on June 22 is now moving forward. Circumstances force
me to bring the two principal players together. The meeting will take place in your
house, tonight at nine o’clock, with your permission. – Salvator That night, Daspry arrived
at eight o’clock, and I showed him the letter. Daspry laughed heartily and said, "Oh,
we must stay and see what happens, my friend." We made sure the doors
were unlocked, and at 8:40, the doorbell rang. "They’re early!" remarked Daspry. I went to
the door and found Madame Andermatt. "My husband is coming," she gasped, rushing in.
"They intend to give him the letters." She explained that a servant had given a
message for her husband to her by mistake. "He grabbed it from me, but
I had read it already. He was told to come here tonight and bring the
document connected with the project. In exchange, he’ll receive the letters." "Does your husband
know you are here?" Daspry asked. She shook her head. Suddenly, the clock struck nine.
"Quickly!" I whispered, leading the others to a velvet curtain in the library. "We
can hide behind here but observe the events of the room." Within moments, we heard
the front door creak open. "Not a word," Daspry warned. Someone entered the library.
I peeked around the curtain and saw Alfred Varin. I recognized him because he resembled
his brother. Varin scrutinized the room carefully, his eyes lingering on the mosaic of
the king and his sword. Suddenly, the door swung open. "You! You brought me here?"
Monsieur Andermatt bellowed as he entered the room. "You sent for me!" shouted Varin.
"No," declared Andermatt. "Someone has lured us both here," said Varin. "I’m leaving." "Wait!" shouted
Andermatt, blocking Varin’s way. "What happened to Lacombe?" "How should I know?" spat Varin.
"Because a few days after he disappeared, you had the submarine plans and tried to
sell them to me. How did you get them?" demanded Andermatt. Varin smiled wickedly.
"All you care about are your wife’s letters. No?" Andermatt’s face grew red. "Yes.
Give them to me." "Only if you give me the final document for the submarine,"
Varin said coldly. He reached into his coat pocket, drew a revolver, and pointed
it at Andermatt. "Hand them over." Suddenly, a pistol shot sounded, and Varin’s weapon dropped
to the floor. Daspry had fired, and in a moment, he was standing between
the two men. "Who are you?" Varin gasped. "The one holding the cards," said Daspry,
holding up the iron plate with the red spots. "You were told to bring
something?" Varin took out a large envelope. "I want twenty thousand francs for the plans."
"Monsieur Andermatt will kindly sign a check in the amount of ten thousand francs,"
said Daspry. Andermatt began to protest, but then obediently wrote out the check. "Now, the
package of letters." "I haven’t got them," Varin replied. "No?" said Daspry. "Open the
hiding place." Daspry held out the iron plate. Varin shook his head vehemently. "Then I
shall." Daspry walked toward the mosaic of the king. He lined up the iron
plate with the edges of the king’s sword, and then punched through its seven holes
with an awl he had in his pocket, pressing on seven of the mosaic’s
stones. There was a clicking sound, and a part of the wall opened, leaving a
large opening. "It’s a safe!" I thought. "It’s empty," said Varin smugly. "And there
is no other hiding place." "There must be. Where is it?" demanded Daspry. Varin thought
a moment and replied, "I want another ten thousand francs." "You’ll have it," said
Andermatt and signed another check. Varin took the plate from Daspry, closed the safe, turned
the plate around, and placed it on the sword again. There was another clicking
sound, and a smaller safe opened. Inside the small safe was a packet of letters.
"Did you bring the final document for the submarine, the Seven-of-Hearts?" asked Daspry. Andermatt
nodded and handed the paper and checks to Daspry. "Then our business has ended," said
Daspry as he gave Andermatt the letters. The banker left without a backward glance.
"My money, monsieur," grumbled Varin. "The money is mine now," Daspry replied coolly. Varin’s face
turned purple, but he remained calm. "Might I ask you a question?" "You may."
"Was there a black case in the large safe?" Daspry nodded. "I found it on
June 22." "Did you take it?" Varin’s voice shook. "It was filled with jewels,"
said Daspry. "Of course I took it." "What is your name?" asked Varin, shaking his
head. Daspry glanced over at where I was hiding. "Arsène Lupin." Varin looked stunned
as he staggered out the door. "Daspry, I mean Lupin—oh, what do I call you?"
I cried, coming out of hiding. "Madame Andermatt has fainted." We rushed over to
her just as she was regaining consciousness. "My letters . . . ," she said
in a small voice. "Do not worry, madame," whispered Lupin, taking a package out
of his pocket. "These are your real letters. I gave your husband fake letters that
will not incriminate you. Go home. Your husband will be happy to see you."
Madame Andermatt clutched the letters and hurried out the door. "I have many questions," I
said when we were alone. "And I am ready to answer them, my friend,"
Lupin said, as we left the library together. The next morning, an article appeared in
the Écho : Arsène Lupin has solved the mystery submitted by Salvator. Having acquired
all the documents for Lacombe’s submarine, he has placed them in the hands of the
minister of the navy. He has also made a generous donation in the sum
of twenty thousand francs for the construction of the submarine. And that is how I
made the acquaintance of Arsène Lupin, gentleman burglar, but more importantly, my dear friend.
Late one winter night, Monsieur Imbert was walking home from a party, his footsteps echoing pleasantly.
But soon, he got the feeling someone was following him. Imbert turned around and thought he
saw a shadow behind a tree, so he quickened his steps. Suddenly, Imbert was attacked from
behind. He shouted for help, but his attacker was too strong and pinned him to the ground.
Luckily, a passerby rushed to help and fought off the assailant. "Are you hurt, sir?" the
rescuer asked, helping Imbert to his feet. Imbert was too shaken to walk, so the man
waved down a cab, helped him into the vehicle, and accompanied Imbert home. "I owe you
my life," said Imbert as they arrived at his mansion. "My wife is asleep, but she
will want to thank you for your heroism. Please come to lunch tomorrow. My name is
Ludovic Imbert." "I am Arsène Lupin," replied the man. Lupin was not yet famous; in fact,
it was for this particular affair that the gentleman burglar invented this name. With the help
of an associate, Lupin had planned this attack for six months, collecting information on the Imberts and
questioning their servants. Finally, his goal was within reach. Soon, Lupin would be in the Imbert
home and near their safe, which was rumored to contain stocks and bonds worth millions! The
next day, Lupin arrived at the mansion and met Gervaise, Imbert's plump and talkative wife. "Welcome,
Monsieur Lupin," she gushed. The Imberts and Lupin spent lunch getting acquainted, and by the time
dessert was served, Lupin knew everything about them. Madame Imbert had inherited millions from a rich
friend named Andrew Brawford, but his nephews were challenging her inheritance. "The bonds and stocks are
in our safe," she lamented, "but we can't sell them until the legalities are resolved." "So the
rumors are true," Lupin thought, thrilled at his proximity to the safe. Out of gratitude, the
Imberts appointed Lupin as their personal secretary when their new friend confessed to being somewhat poor.
Lupin was given an office on the second floor, directly above Imbert's office and the safe.
But Lupin noticed quickly that his position involved very little actual work. In two months, he
wrote only four letters and was never called into his employer's office. He never socialized with
the Imberts, and the servants didn't talk to him. Lupin did not complain, since he preferred
to spend his time working on a plan. He made secret visits to Imbert's office to inspect
the safe, a large block of iron that could only be opened with both a combination
and a key. "Where force fails, cunning prevails," Lupin said to himself. He bored a hole
through the floor of his room to penetrate the ceiling of Imbert's office. Then he inserted
a pipe through the hole so he could see and hear what transpired in the room
below. Stretched out on the floor, Lupin often saw the couple in front of the safe,
examining books and papers. Whenever they twisted the combination lock, Lupin watched, trying to learn the
numbers. One day, the couple left the office without locking the safe, and Lupin quickly went
downstairs. On entering the room, however, he saw they had abruptly returned. "I beg your pardon," Lupin
said deftly. "I must have opened the wrong door." Gervaise ran up to him. "Come in,
I'm glad you're here." "We want your advice," murmured Imbert. "Should we sell some of the
bonds or stocks?" "But I thought Brawford's nephews prevented you from selling," said Lupin, surprised. "Oh,
their lawsuit doesn't involve all our holdings," answered Gervaise. The shelves inside the safe were filled
with bundles of stocks and bonds, and she took one out. "Not those stocks, Gervaise," her
husband protested. "They're not selling well right now. But the government bonds might turn a profit.
What do you think, Lupin?" "I agree with you," said Lupin, even though he had no idea
which ones to sell or keep. But that afternoon, Imbert and Lupin sold some of the
bonds for 46,000 francs. "Imagine how much money all of them would fetch!" thought Lupin. To
complicate matters, stories accusing the Imberts of being swindlers appeared in the press, which threw the
entire household into uncertainty. Lupin decided he must act, or he would lose everything. During the
next five days, instead of leaving the mansion at six o'clock as usual, Lupin would lock
himself in his office. He lay on the floor, watching Imbert's office, hoping for a chance
to steal the stocks and bonds. On the sixth day, Lupin got his chance. The couple, upset
by the press accounts, decided to review the safe's contents. Lupin spied on them for hours
that evening, and when the servants went to bed, Lupin decided to make his move. "It's
now or never," he murmured. Using a knotted rope, he climbed out of his window and
quietly dropped down to the balcony of the office window below. "I'm tired," Gervaise complained. "Don't
worry. I'll finish up," said her husband. Earlier, Lupin had unlocked the office windows so he
could enter easily. When he heard Gervaise leave, he opened the window slightly, and the curtain
billowed with the night breeze. "It's cold in here," Imbert remarked and rose to close the
window. As soon as Imbert neared the window, Lupin wrapped the man's head in the curtain and
tied him up before Imbert could see his assailant. Then, Lupin ran to the open safe
and put the bundles of stocks and bonds into a cloth sack he had previously hidden.
He raced upstairs to his office, removed the rope, and covered the hole in the floor.
Lupin exited through the servant's gate, where a carriage was waiting for him. Examining the bundles
a few hours later , Lupin said to his associate, "These won't add up to millions,
but we'll still collect a respectable sum." The next morning, Lupin read a startling headline in
the newspaper. "'Ludovic and Gervaise Imbert have disappeared,'" read Lupin aloud. The police had raided the Imbert
mansion only moments after Lupin had left and found the home empty. These are the facts
as Arsène Lupin related them to me much later, pacing nervously up and down in my
study. "There are some things I still don't understand about this affair," he confided. "For example,
why did the Imberts flee? They could have said they were robbed. The safe was empty."
"Did you ever see them again?" I asked. Lupin shook his head. "Maybe you're feeling regret,"
I said. "You stole their fortune." "What fortune?" Lupin shouted. "All their stocks and bonds were
counterfeit! Fakes! The Imberts played me for a fool!" I stared at him, dumbfounded. "Unknown to me,
I was playing a role from the very beginning. Reading the newspapers after their disappearance, I
realized they had been passing me off as one of Andrew Brawford's nephews," said Lupin. "You
see, they told their acquaintances that the lawsuit was over. No one knew my real name
or quite what I did there. So, thanks to my existence, the Imberts were able to
borrow money from everyone." "Because they thought the Imberts would soon be able to access their
funds!" I added, finally understanding how the couple's scheme worked. "And worst of all, that woman
borrowed 1,500 francs from me! I gave her my life savings willingly, thinking I would steal
millions from her in return . . ." Lupin sat down and buried his face in his
hands. "Are you all right, old chap?" I asked, worried. Then my friend raised his head
and burst into laughter at the great joke that had been played on him. The novice
gentleman burglar had learned a valuable lesson on his way to becoming the great Arsène Lupin.
The doorbell awakened the guard of the quiet apartment building. He glanced at his watch.
It was three o'clock in the morning. "It must be an emergency for the doctor on
the third floor," he murmured as he got up to open the door for the
visitor. Once inside, the visitor silently ascended the stairs, and without stopping at the third floor,
proceeded up to the fifth floor. There he tried two keys in the lock. One
of them fit. "Perfect," he said, and he waited a few minutes before descending to the
lobby. "That's enough time for the guard to assume I have seen the doctor," he
thought. The visitor exited the building noisily so the guard would believe he had left, but
he stuck something in the lock so it would not bolt. A few minutes later,
he quietly entered again, went up to the fifth floor, and sneaked into the dark apartment.
He took out a floor plan of the apartment and shined a flashlight on it.
"This corridor leads to the bedrooms," he thought. "A closet door connects to the countess' bedroom."
He turned off the flashlight and walked to the closet. He was about to pick
the lock, but the door opened easily. "You are lucky, Lupin," he whispered to himself. He
stepped inside the closet and easily picked the lock on the door leading to the
bedroom. "According to the floor plan," thought Lupin, "there's a small table by the bed. The
black pearl will be inside a box of stationery on that table." The Countess Zalti,
whose bedroom floor Lupin now was creeping across, had once been the most admired woman in
Paris. She had owned exquisite jewelry, worn fine clothes, and traveled to exotic places, but
then lost her fortune and now had just a small apartment, a manservant, and a housekeeper.
To sustain herself, she had sold all her jewels except for the famous black pearl.
It was worth more than all the other jewels combined, and she would not part with
it. Lupin had almost reached the table when his fingers touched something on the floor.
"An overturned candlestick? Strange!" he thought. Then his hand brushed against something else—hair, and after that
an ice-cold face. Lupin froze and nearly screamed. "Countess Zalti," he whispered. He quickly turned
on his flashlight, stood up, and surveyed the room. He saw signs of a struggle—an overturned
chair, a small clock with its hands stopped at 11:20. Then, his heart beating wildly,
he saw the countess lying motionless on the floor, with a red gash across her neck.
Blood was everywhere. "She's dead," thought Lupin. Then he remembered the black pearl and looked
in the box of stationery. It was empty! Lupin collapsed onto a chair to think.
Forty minutes later he left the building. Countess Zalti and her famous black pearl were once
again in the newspapers—this time, however, because of her gruesome murder. The newspapers reported that
her manservant, Victor Danègre, had been arrested. Upon searching his room, the chief of police, Dudouis,
had found a coat stained with a few drops of blood hidden under his mattress.
Later a missing button from that coat was found under the countess' bed. However, some points
needed further explanation. Witnesses said Danègre went to a tobacco shop at seven o'clock in
the morning. But the countess' housekeeper testified that the door was locked when she rose at
eight o'clock. Danègre did not have a key, so how did he leave the apartment
and lock the door after himself? The police's investigation turned up no answers—only new mysteries. The
countess' cousin declared that a month before her death, the countess had written to her
and described the exact location of the black pearl. That letter, however, had disappeared the next
day. The building's guard recalled a visitor for the doctor, but the doctor testified he
had seen no one. There were too many suspects in the case and not enough evidence,
so the police had to free Danègre. During the six-month investigation, Danègre had been in
prison. Upon release he was physically and mentally weak, a shadow of his former self. Because
of the publicity, he couldn't get a job, so he changed his name to Anatole
Dufour. One evening, as he was eating dinner at a cafe, a man wearing a black
raincoat entered and sat at his table. The man poured them both some wine. "To
your health, Victor Danègre," the man toasted. "You are mistaken. My name is Dufour." The man
shook his head and said, "I am Grimaudan, ex-detective, and you are Victor Danègre, ex-servant
of the deceased Countess Zalti." "What do you want?" growled Danègre. "I've been sent by the
countess' cousin," replied Grimaudan, "to recover the black pearl." "I don't have it," said Danègre.
"Oh yes, you do," Grimaudan retorted. "The police couldn't prove it," insisted Danègre. Grimaudan took a
sip of wine. "Three weeks before the murder, you took the countess' key and paid
the locksmith to make a copy." "That's a lie!" shouted Danègre. Grimaudan took the key out
of his pocket. "You killed the countess with a knife you bought from a shop
the same day you duplicated the key," continued Grimaudan. "No!" cried Danègre. Again Grimaudan reached
into his pocket. He took out the knife. "You have a key and a knife. Who
can prove they belong to me?" said Danègre, regaining his composure. "The locksmith and the
clerk at the shop will identify you," replied Grimaudan coldly. Danègre's mouth went dry. "It's been
too long. They could never remember all their customers." "Perhaps. But there is more evidence
that will convict you of this terrible crime—your fingerprint." Danègre started to argue, but Grimaudan continued.
"After you murdered the countess, you left through the closet. You were scared, unsteady, and
leaned against the wall for support. Your thumb, wet with blood, made an impression on the
wall. If I direct the police to that fingerprint, they will see it matches yours."
Danègre hung his head. "How much will you give me for the pearl?" "Nothing," replied Grimaudan.
"I will give you your life." "I will take you to it," said Danègre. They
walked out of the restaurant and toward the countess' former apartment building, finally stopping in front
of a bench. "It's here." "Where?" Grimaudan looked around but didn't see anything. Danègre remained
silent. "You still want me to pay you for the pearl," Grimaudan remarked. "How much?" "Just
enough to get me to America," Danègre replied. "Agreed," said Grimaudan. "Now where is it?"
"See the pavement stones? Count the stones to the right of the sewer grate. The pearl
is between the twelfth and thirteenth stones." Grimaudan counted the stones. When he got to
the spot, he took out a knife and thrust it between the stones, digging deeply. His
knife struck something, and he enlarged the hole with his finger. Finally Grimaudan pulled the
pearl out of its filthy hiding place. The following day the Écho printed this article: Yesterday
the famous black pearl fell into the hands of Arsène Lupin, who acquired it from
the murderer of the Countess Zalti. Soon the precious jewel will be exhibited around the world
for all to admire. Lupin is prepared to receive offers for the jewel. Lupin and
I discussed the affair over dinner one evening. "I had enough time in the countess' bedroom
to form a plan to catch the murderer and retrieve the black pearl," explained Lupin.
"I decided that Danègre had to be arrested but not convicted. So I made sure the
police found Danègre's button, but not the knife and key. I also wiped off the
fingerprint in the closet." "And poor Danègre fell right into your trap," I said. "And this
fell right into my hands." Lupin's eyes twinkled as he held up the black pearl.
"Meet Arsène Lupin!" joked Georges Devanne, a wealthy banker, as he presented Horace Velmont, a friend. The
introduction was met with laughter by his guests, who were at Thibermesnil Castle. "There is an
uncanny resemblance," remarked Father Gelis, one of the guests. "But I did hear that Lupin has been
spotted in this area." The gentleman who was the object of their laughter did in fact
look rather like Lupin. He stood quietly, wearing a bemused smile. "I first met Velmont," Devanne continued,
nodding toward his smiling friend, "three months ago at a casino in Dieppe. He is a talented
painter, and my brother knows his work well. He has visited my home several times since
then, but he has never crept around in the middle of the night. At least I don't
think so." This speech provoked another eruption of laughter, and then the guests followed Devanne into
the gallery, which occupied the entire first floor of the castle. This gallery contained Devanne's growing collection
of antiques and paintings, plus an immense bookcase. At the top of the bookcase, the name of
the castle was spelled out in gold: Thibermesnil. After the guests lit their cigars, Devanne resumed
the conversation. "Velmont, if you are going to rob me, tonight is your last chance." "Why is
that?" Velmont grinned. Devanne took a sip of his wine before answering casually, "I'm expecting a
visitor tomorrow afternoon at four o'clock—Sherlock Holmes, the famous English detective." At first the guests were speechless;
then they began asking questions all at once. "Is Holmes really coming?" "Is Lupin truly in the
neighborhood?" "Did you get a warning letter like Baron Cahorn?" Devanne laughed. "Lupin and his band
are not far away, I suspect," said Devanne. "And Lupin would not use the same trick twice.
However, I know he's up to something. That's why I sent for the great detective himself."
"What's Lupin planning?" asked Velmont. Devanne walked to the bookcase and said, "These books contain the history
of the Thibermesnil family." Then he pointed to an empty space on the shelf. "As you can
see, one book is missing—the book detailing the construction of the castle. That volume describes a
secret underground tunnel, with an entrance somewhere in this room. The book disappeared a month ago." "A
lost book hardly seems a sufficient reason for summoning Sherlock Holmes," commented Velmont. "Ordinarily I would
agree," said Devanne, "but there was another copy in the National Library in Paris, which contained details
about the secret tunnel not included in my book. In other words, one would need both books
in order to determine the exact location of the tunnel." "Let me guess," interjected Velmont. "That
book has also disappeared." Devanne nodded. "And you believe Lupin is behind this?" asked Father Gelis. "Yes.
When I explained the situation to Holmes, he was eager to match wits with Arsène Lupin,"
Devanne replied. "What an honor for Lupin," said Velmont. "But what if Lupin is not planning to
rob you?" "Holmes is also interested in solving the mystery of the secret tunnel," said Devanne. "Can
you remember anything about the tunnel from the missing book?" asked Velmont. Devanne nodded. "For centuries
the castle lords waited until they lay on their deathbeds to pass on the tunnel's location to
their sons. The last of the lords of Thibermesnil was beheaded in the French Revolution at
the age of 19, and he had no children. Since then others, including me, have tried to
find the tunnel—without success. The house plans in the book at the National Library showed a series
of stairs with a total of 48 steps, which descend more than ten meters." "That would
mean the tunnel runs underneath the old moat surrounding this castle ," exclaimed Velmont. "And ends within
the walls of this room," said Devanne. "But where exactly does it lie? The mystery remains."
"Do not forget the two quotations, Monsieur Devanne," prompted Father Gelis. Devanne laughed. "Father Gelis has been
interested in Thibermesnil for many years. He came across a cryptic quote in the church archives. But
I must say, it only confuses the matter." "What's the quote?" asked Velmont. "Well, legend has
it that Henry IV spent a night in this castle just before a famous battle," began Devanne.
"His mistress was brought to him through the tunnel. The king confided the secret location to
his minister, saying, ‘Turn one eye on the bee that shakes; the other eye will lead to
God.'" "It doesn't make sense," said Velmont. "It's code, monsieur," Father Gelis said hotly. "Obviously Henry IV
did not want anyone to know the whereabouts of the secret tunnel." "Father Gelis also discovered
a note in Louis XVI's famous jewelry chest in the Louvre; it read ‘Thibermesnil 3-4-11,'" said Devanne.
"Ah! The magic key," Velmont said sarcastically. "Now, who can fit the key into the invisible
lock?" Father Gelis stiffened his shoulders. "Laugh as much as you like, but I'm confident those two
clues are the key to the location of the tunnel." "Sherlock Holmes will figure it out, I'm
sure," added Devanne. Velmont shook Devanne's hand. "I think your book and the one in the
library lacked a very important detail," he said, smiling broadly, "which you just supplied. Now I can
plunder your castle." "You'll have to hurry, Monsieur Lupin ." Devanne chuckled. "Sherlock Holmes arrives tomorrow."
"Then it shall have to be tonight," Velmont replied with a wink. "By the way, I can
drive you to Dieppe this evening," Devanne said. "I am meeting some friends and a young lady
they know at the train station. They will be staying with me." An hour later Devanne
and Velmont were driving toward Dieppe. Devanne dropped off Velmont and then picked up his friends at
the train station. The castle remained in darkness until the clock struck three in the morning.
Suddenly there was a clicking noise in the gallery, and a thin stream of light flashed from
the bookcase. Then the room flooded with light as a whole section of the bookcase rotated to
reveal a large opening. Arsène Lupin walked into the room carrying a flashlight, followed by eight
men carrying various tools and a coil of rope. Lupin passed quickly from one piece of furniture
to another and instructed his accomplices whether to take it or leave it. In just forty
minutes, the best pieces from the room had been removed in an orderly and noiseless manner, and
the men exited the same way they had entered. Lupin pushed the bookcase back into place after
them and carefully removed all traces of the men's footsteps and fingerprints from the gallery. Next
he walked down a corridor to a glass cabinet containing a priceless collection of watches, rings, and
figurines. Lupin picked the lock and began to fill his pockets with the miniature treasures, but
a faint noise startled him. He remembered there was a guest room at the end of the
corridor, where one of the friends Devanne had picked up that evening was probably sleeping. Lupin quickly
extinguished his flashlight and had just hidden behind a curtain when the guest-room door opened. Lupin
saw a woman walking down the corridor. She appeared nervous; the candle she carried shook slightly. She
passed so close that her skirt brushed against the curtain and he could smell her perfume.
Then, without warning, she stopped and pulled the curtain aside. Lupin was dumbstruck. "Miss Nelly," he whispered.
Arsène Lupin was frozen in place. Standing before him was the lovely Miss Nelly!
The same charming creature who, rather than betray him on the ship, had
dropped the camera hiding the diamonds into the water. "I dreamed of seeing you
again one day," Lupin finally said. Her eyes moved to his hands, which were
filled with jewelry. She shuddered and ran into the gallery. "Please, I can
explain," cried Lupin, embarrassed to be caught like a common thief. He followed and
found her trembling at the sight of the devastated room. "Tomorrow, at three o'clock,
everything will be returned," he said. "I promise." Suddenly she spoke. "Listen .
. . footsteps. You must go." She ran toward the door to the gallery
and listened. When she turned around, Arsène Lupin was gone. Early the next morning,
Devanne was informed about the robbery, and he immediately thought, "Velmont is Lupin!"
But then he reconsidered. "It's ridiculous to suspect the famous painter." The police could
find no clues—except one. The castle's missing book had been restored to the
bookcase, and next to it was the book missing from the National Library. Devanne's
friends arrived at 11 o'clock to provide support and to satisfy their curiosity; the
only friend not present was Velmont, which aroused Devanne's suspicions again. But the
suspected thief appeared at noon. "Velmont!" Devanne cried. "Surprised to see me?" Velmont asked
innocently. "Yes, since you robbed me last night," said Devanne. "Nonsense!" exclaimed Velmont pleasantly.
He was introduced to Devanne's new guests and Miss Nelly and smiled at

the entrance to the castle. They talked about the robbery and the imminent arrival
