located your belongings." Excited, Devanne and his guests ran outside. He peered under
the wagon covers to behold his stolen treasures. "We received an anonymous note telling
us where to find them," explained the officer. During the commotion Miss Nelly had
remained on the terrace. But she was not alone. "I kept my promise,"
Lupin whispered. She just stood there, silent. "Forget that I'm a thief," he begged.
"Remember those wonderful days when I was Bernard d'Andrézy. Please?" She pointed to a
ring on his finger. The ring belonged to Georges Devanne. "You are right."
He smiled bitterly. "Arsène Lupin is now and always will be Arsène Lupin." He
bowed as she walked away, never to see her again. "I must leave before
Sherlock Holmes arrives," he thought, running out a back door and through the
woods behind the castle. Back on the road, he soon encountered a tall man
carrying a cane. "Excuse me, is this the way to the castle?" the
man asked in an English accent. "Yes," replied Lupin. "They are expecting you, Mr.
Holmes." Sherlock Holmes scrutinized Lupin from head to foot. Suddenly two policemen on horses
galloped by, forcing the two men into the bushes to avoid being trampled.
The two remarkable men emerged and brushed themselves off. Then, without a word, they
parted and went their separate ways—two opposing forces of nature that had been destined
to meet face-to-face for just a moment. "Ah, you are here. I am
delighted to meet you!" cried Devanne when Holmes walked up to the castle. "Did
my chauffeur meet you at the station?" "I preferred to walk," grumbled Holmes. Devanne
forced a smile and proceeded to explain the events of the night before.
Holmes turned to leave. "Where are you going?" asked Devanne. "Home," the Englishman replied.
"But why?" "Your goods have been returned and Lupin is gone. There is nothing
for me to do." "But I need your help!" Devanne cried. "We do
not know how he got in or why he returned the goods." Holmes removed
his hat and said, "Tell me everything." Devanne escorted the detective to the gallery,
showed him the returned books, and explained about the secret tunnel. Holmes asked
questions about everything. "Was yesterday the first time you spoke about the two quotes?"
Holmes asked. "Yes," replied Devanne. "Prepare to take me back to the station in
an hour," Holmes said confidently. "That is how long it took Lupin to
solve this mystery, and so it shall be with me." He paced the room,
in deep thought, and then sat down and closed his eyes. After a few
minutes, he said, "Is there a chapel near the castle?" "Yes, but—" "Tell
your driver to wait for me there," interrupted Holmes. "Do you think the tunnel
runs to the chapel?" asked Devanne, ignoring Holmes' request. "Now, bring me a ladder
and a flashlight," ordered Holmes. Devanne rushed to provide what the detective requested.
"Place the ladder against the bookcase to the left of the word ‘Thibermesnil,'" he
instructed. Devanne obeyed. "Climb up and turn the first letter I ," Holmes
continued. "It turns to the right," Devanne cried excitedly. "Take the letter B and
move it back and forth," ordered Holmes. When Devanne did that, there was a
clicking sound. "Now, move the ladder to the other end of the word
'Thibermesnil' and pull the other letter I ," said Holmes. Devanne pulled the letter,
and an entire section of the bookcase opened, pushing him off the ladder. Unhurt,
Devanne stared into the dark opening. "The secret tunnel!" "Turn one eye on
the bee that shakes; the other eye will lead to God," said Holmes. "Turn
the first I in Thibermesnil, shake the B , then pull the other I
. Just to remind himself, Louis XVI wrote 3-4-11 . . . the
third, fourth, and eleventh letters of the name." Devanne gazed at Holmes with admiration
as the detective stepped into the tunnel. "From inside here the reverse side of
the letters can be reached," Holmes said. "Lupin worked the combination that way
to get inside." "Then he knows the other entrance," cried Devanne. "Yes, and I
do too," said Holmes as he continued down the tunnel, with Devanne following. First
they descended a stairway of 48 steps and then walked through a long,
damp passageway. At last the men came to another stairway of 48 steps and
ascended to a granite wall, which Holmes examined. "Aha!" he exclaimed when he saw
the word "Thibermesnil" in reverse on the wall. Holmes used the same combination,
and the large block of granite opened into the old chapel. On the other
side, the granite formed a tomb with the word "Thibermesnil" engraved on it. "The
other eye leads to God," said Holmes. "This chapel." Devanne clapped his hands
excitedly. The two men emerged from the chapel to find Devanne's automobile waiting for
them. "How did you know to come here?" Devanne asked the driver. "Monsieur
Velmont told me," answered the man. "He knew you would solve the mystery," said
Devanne to Holmes. A smile of satisfaction lit up the detective's face. "I knew
Lupin was clever when I saw him." "You saw Lupin?" asked Devanne. "On
my way to the castle," Holmes replied. "You didn't stop him?" exclaimed Devanne. Ignoring
him, Holmes got into the automobile and saw a package addressed to him on
the seat. "What is it?" asked Devanne. Holmes opened the package, took out
a watch, and frowned. He recalled the horses forcing him and Lupin into the
bushes. Devanne began laughing. "Arsène Lupin stole your watch. Now he returns it!" "Yes,
he is a clever man," Holmes said. "And one day I shall have
the pleasure of meeting him again. Yes, Sherlock Holmes will meet Arsène Lupin again."
